B01:
RAG versus fine-tuning comes up in almost every conversation about adapting a language model to a specific job, and the two get treated as interchangeable more often than they should. They solve different problems, and picking wrong costs real time and money, and usually accuracy too.

The short version: RAG is for freshness and citations. Because it pulls answers from a live knowledge base at query time, the model can reference documents that changed yesterday and point users to exact sources. Fine-tuning is for style and latency. It bakes knowledge and tone into the model's weights, so responses come back faster and more consistent, with no retrieval step.

The example that makes the trade-off concrete: a customer-support knowledge base with 100,000 documents. Do you retrieve from it, fine-tune on it, or both? The answer depends on how often the content changes, how much citations matter, and how long your users will wait. The rest of this post works through that decision.
B02:
The reflex answer to a slow Postgres query is to add an index. It usually works, which is why tables accumulate indexes the way junk drawers accumulate batteries. Every one of them has a cost, and the cost lands on your writes.

Unused indexes are the most common version of this. Every INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE has to maintain every index on the table, so an index that never serves a single query is still doing work on every write, taking up storage, and stretching out your vacuum cycles.

A recent client made the point for us. One of their core tables had picked up 23 indexes over the years. We audited them and dropped 14. Write throughput doubled. No hardware changes, no query rewrites, just less work per write.

This post covers the indexing pitfalls we see most often, how to find unused indexes in your own database, and a checklist for keeping things lean.
B03:
Every company claims to have remote onboarding figured out, right up until a new hire spends their first week waiting for access, hunting for documentation, and wondering who to ask for help. On a distributed team those small frictions compound, because nobody is sitting nearby to notice you're stuck.

We onboarded 27 remote hires over the past year, made plenty of mistakes, and ran plenty of experiments along the way. Time-to-first-PR went from 12 days to 5, which means new engineers now ship real code in their first week instead of their third.

This guide is the playbook that got us there: how we structure the first day, what onboarding buddies actually do, which documentation matters and which doesn't, and the metrics we track to keep improving.
B04:
How are design systems actually doing inside the organizations that build them? For The State of Design Systems 2026, we surveyed 412 designers across industries, company sizes, and levels of design maturity. The headline number is blunt: 61% say their design system is partially adopted at best.

For most teams, in other words, the design system exists but is not the single source of truth it was meant to be. The reasons are familiar: unclear ownership, competing priorities, gaps between design and code, documentation that drifts out of date. The data also shows what works. Teams that get adoption right share some surprisingly consistent habits.

The report that follows unpacks the numbers, the trends shaping design systems in 2026, and the takeaways worth bringing back to your own team.
B05:
Building an emergency fund is not glamorous. There is no dopamine hit, no compounding chart to admire, and nobody brags about their savings account at parties. It is still the one financial move that reliably pays off.

The standard advice says to set aside 3 to 6 months of expenses, enough cushion to absorb a job loss, a medical bill, or a surprise car repair without reaching for a credit card. Simple to state. For most people, genuinely hard to do.

I know because it took me 14 months to build mine on a $52k salary. What I learned along the way is that the hard part is not the math. It's the habits, the trade-offs, and staying motivated while the balance grows painfully slowly.

This post is exactly how I did it: the budget changes that mattered most, the automation that kept me consistent, and the mindset shifts that kept me going. If you've been putting off starting, or you started and stalled, I hope this reads as a realistic roadmap rather than a lecture.

The average mid-market company uses 7 different tools just for purchasing: spreadsheets, email threads, ERP modules, standalone approval apps. Procurement is usually the last place companies look for efficiency gains, which is exactly why so much inefficiency hides there.

The day-to-day result is a process nobody defends. Requests get lost between systems. Approvers don't know what's waiting for them. Finance can't see committed spend. A simple purchase turns into a multi-week ordeal.

Consolidating requests, approvals, and vendor management into a single workflow changes the numbers quickly. Companies that make the switch routinely watch 14-day approval cycles drop to 3.

This post looks at how procurement tooling got so fragmented, what a consolidated setup looks like in practice, and how to tell whether your organization is ready to change.
B08:
On Tuesday our platform went down for 4 hours, affecting a significant portion of our users. The root cause was an expired TLS certificate on an internal service that sat squarely in our request path. This postmortem explains what happened and what we're changing.

The short version is humbling. A certificate we didn't realize was close to expiry, on a service most of us rarely thought about, expired quietly and took a surprising amount of our stack down with it. Alerts fired, but the failure mode was confusing, and tracing the cascading errors back to their source took longer than it should have.

Below we walk through the full timeline, the contributing factors, and the 3 action items we're committing to: automated certificate-expiry monitoring across all services, documented rotation runbooks for every internal certificate, and regular game-day testing of certificate failure modes.

We're publishing the details because we'd rather other teams learn this from our outage than from their own.

The old objection to vertical software was market size. A niche industry might desperately need better tools, but if the TAM couldn't support a venture-scale outcome, investors passed. AI changes that math. When a small team can build, sell, and support software that used to require fifty people, small vertical markets become viable, and in some cases attractive.

Marina software is a good example: a $400M TAM most funds would have ignored a decade ago. An AI-native team can now serve that market profitably at a fraction of the old cost structure, own the core workflow end to end, and expand into payments, insurance, and adjacent services over time.

Our thesis: the next generation of great vertical SaaS companies will be smaller teams attacking smaller markets and capturing far more of them. If you're building in this space, we'd like to hear from you.

T01:
I sent thousands of cold emails last year and ended at an 8% reply rate. Five lessons that got me there:

1/ Keep it to 4 lines. Your prospect is scanning on their phone between meetings. Four lines is enough to say who you are, why you're relevant, and what you want. Anything longer gets archived.

2/ One CTA. Every additional ask cuts your response rate. "Worth a 15-min chat?" beats a menu of options.

3/ Personalize the first line, and make it real. "Loved your post on X" only works if you actually read the post. One genuine sentence beats five templated ones.

4/ Follow up. Most replies come from the 2nd or 3rd email, not the 1st. A polite bump is how deals happen, and silence is not a no.

5/ Track subject lines, send times, and CTAs. The 8% reply rate only happened after I started treating cold email as a system instead of a lottery. Iterate weekly.
T02: Most meetings should be memos. Writing forces clarity, respects everyone's time, and leaves a record you can search. An idea that can't survive being written down won't survive a 60-minute meeting either.
T03:
19 months ago I launched a $49 one-time product. This week we crossed $10k MRR. No funding, no team, no audience. The playbook, in 4 tweets:

1/ Start ugly. V1 was a $49 one-time purchase: no subscriptions, no dashboard, barely a landing page. It made a handful of sales, which was the point. It proved people would pay. Validation first, polish later.

2/ Listen for the pivot. Customers kept returning with the same recurring problem, and a one-time product couldn't serve it. Month 7, we moved to subscriptions. Revenue dipped for a few weeks, then compounded.

3/ Do things that don't scale. I onboarded every early customer personally, answered every support email, and asked every churned user why they left. Those conversations wrote the roadmap.

4/ 19 months to $10k MRR is not a rocket ship, and that's fine. Slow, profitable, compounding growth is still growth. If you're bootstrapping right now, keep going. It adds up.

T05:
Can LLMs judge other LLMs? A new paper tests "LLM-as-judge" against human evaluators. Short answer: useful for routine tasks, shaky for creative ones. 4 findings:

1/ Overall, LLM judges agree with human evaluators 81% of the time. For routine evaluation tasks, an LLM judge is a reasonable stand-in for a human rater.

2/ On creative tasks, agreement drops to 64%. Where there is no objectively correct answer (style, originality, taste), LLM judges and humans part ways.

3/ One likely culprit: judges reward surface features like structure, fluency, and length over actual creativity. They like writing that looks good more than writing that is good.

4/ Use LLM-as-judge for scale on objective tasks, and keep humans in the loop for creative work. 81% is not 100%, and 64% is uncomfortably close to a coin flip.

R01: Automated code review has the potential to reduce defect rates and reviewer workload, yet existing tools remain limited in scope and precision. We present ReviewBot, an automated code-review system that combines static analysis with learned models to surface defects within the pull-request workflow. We evaluate ReviewBot on 1,200 pull requests from 8 repositories spanning multiple languages and project sizes. ReviewBot caught 34% more defects than baseline linters, with a 12% false-positive rate that developers in our study described as acceptable for day-to-day use. An analysis by defect category shows the largest gains on cross-file inconsistencies and API-misuse patterns that traditional linters routinely miss. We discuss practical considerations for deploying automated review at scale, including reviewer trust, alert fatigue, and integration with existing continuous-integration pipelines. Our findings suggest that automated code review can meaningfully augment, though not replace, human reviewers. We outline future work on adaptive precision thresholds and repository-specific tuning, and we release our evaluation framework to support reproducibility.
R02:
We surveyed 156 enterprises across industries and regions about their data-governance practices, challenges, and priorities.

The findings show a substantial maturity gap. Most notably, 44% of surveyed enterprises have no data-classification policy, which leaves them unable to consistently identify which data is sensitive, regulated, or business-critical. Without classification as a foundation, downstream controls such as access management, retention, encryption, and incident response rest on guesswork rather than policy.

The gap has measurable costs. Organizations without foundational governance report longer audit cycles, higher breach-response costs, and growing friction as AI initiatives demand well-understood, well-labeled data.

To close it, this whitepaper recommends a 5-step maturity model that takes organizations from initial data discovery through classification, ownership, policy enforcement, and continuous monitoring. Each step includes concrete milestones and self-assessment criteria for benchmarking progress.
R03:
At pilot firms using AI-assisted contract review, review time is down 60%. Work that used to consume days of associate attention now takes hours, which frees legal teams for negotiation strategy and higher-value counsel. For legal ops leaders under pressure to do more with less, that number is why the technology is getting a serious look.

The caveat matters as much as the number: hallucinated citations. AI tools can generate authorities that look entirely plausible and do not exist, and courts have shown little patience with filings that include them. Every AI-assisted output still needs qualified human review.

The professional guardrails are forming too. The ABA has issued guidance on lawyers' use of generative AI, with emphasis on competence, confidentiality, and supervision. Adopt the technology, but own the output.

For legal teams starting now: pick high-volume, lower-risk workflows like contract review, measure the results, and keep lawyers reviewing everything the tools produce. The firms doing this well are pairing AI's speed with a lawyer's judgment.

What has your team seen with AI in legal ops? Tell me in the comments.
